pre_giveup_story.base: respondents who volunteered a free-text answer describing their last give-up (18 of 61 eligible respondents; this field was optional so the other 43 left it blank — themes below describe this self-selected subsample of 18, not all eligible respondents).

themes.paraphrase: Several respondents said that when deciding dragged they left the app entirely — opening YouTube or Instagram instead of continuing to browse Netflix.
themes.implication: Corroborates the C4 off-platform leak measured quantitatively; the leak destination named unprompted is consistently YouTube or social video.

themes.paraphrase: Some respondents said they gave up searching and put on something they'd already seen rather than picking something new.
themes.implication: A 'quick rewatch' shortcut already exists informally; the prototype's 'shows already watched' component maps directly onto this coping behaviour.

themes.theme: Time pressure from the meal itself
themes.paraphrase: A few respondents described the meal finishing, or food going cold, before they had settled on something to watch.
themes.implication: The meal is a hard deadline, not just a mood — supports treating 'meal-window cost' as a real cost, not only an annoyance rating.

themes.paraphrase: A couple of respondents said they never face this because they choose what to watch before sitting down.
themes.implication: Direct qualitative echo of the C3 falsifier segment; this behaviour is a real substitute, not just a survey artifact.

themes.paraphrase: A couple of respondents described browsing around — food content, or simply not having a next show queued — without landing on anything.
themes.implication: Supports a queueing/continuation feature, not just faster search, for the post-finale moment.

themes.paraphrase: One respondent noted difficulty finding something suitable to watch with parents.
themes.implication: A minority but distinct segment (shared viewing) whose friction is about suitability, not volume of choice; too small a signal to size here.

post_one_thing.base: of 37 post respondents, 35 gave a substantive answer to 'what is the ONE thing that would make you actually use it'.

themes.paraphrase: The largest single group asked for recommendations more closely matched to their own taste and watch history, several explicitly contrasting this with the prototype's current suggestions.
themes.implication: Recommendation relevance is the single biggest lever on stated adoption — consistent with the weak 29.4%(prior report)/current-data top-box headline desirability; this is the primary 'improve' target, not a new component.

themes.paraphrase: A number of respondents pointed to the mood filter as the thing they want more of or that already works for them.
themes.implication: Corroborates the quantitative component-usefulness ranking, where mood filters is the second most-cited useful part.

themes.theme: Adapting to meal context (episode length / time of day)
themes.paraphrase: A few respondents wanted the row to account for how long they actually have — for example shorter episodes so the show can finish with the meal.
themes.implication: A concrete, buildable refinement: surface episode runtime and bias toward meal-length content.

themes.theme: Less cognitive effort / fewer choices to weigh
themes.paraphrase: Some respondents said the appeal is simply not having to think — clicking something already picked for them.
themes.implication: Validates the core mechanic (pre-narrowing choice) independent of recommendation quality.

themes.paraphrase: A couple of respondents compared the desired experience to short-form video feeds such as YouTube Shorts.
themes.implication: A different product shape (bite-sized clips) than the current best-episode-pick mechanic; worth flagging as a distinct idea to test, not folding into the current feature.

themes.paraphrase: One respondent found it hard to identify shows from cover art alone and wanted titles shown.
themes.implication: Minor UI fix, low cost, plausibly affects the 'about the same' speed-perception segment.

themes.theme: Already decides in advance — feature doesn't apply
themes.paraphrase: One respondent restated that they plan ahead regardless of platform, so the feature has little to add for them.
themes.implication: Same falsifier segment reappearing in the post survey — this group is unlikely to adopt regardless of iteration.

themes.paraphrase: A handful of answers were non-answers or unrelated one-word replies (e.g. uncertainty about the question, or unrelated words).
themes.implication: Signals response-quality noise in this open field; treat single-word answers as low-confidence evidence.

post_confusion.base: only 4 of 37 post respondents reported anything confusing or in the way; 33 left this blank or wrote 'no' / 'nothing'.

themes.theme: Prototype fidelity blurred the test (felt too much like real Netflix)
themes.paraphrase: Two respondents said the prototype resembled the real Netflix UI closely enough that it was unclear what they were meant to be evaluating, and one wanted a brief orientation before starting.
themes.implication: A study-design note more than a product finding: low reported confusion may partly reflect respondents not clearly distinguishing the feature from the baseline UI, which argues for treating the strongly positive reaction numbers with some caution.

themes.theme: Wants a persistently visible, dedicated section
themes.paraphrase: One respondent suggested a clearly dedicated 'Watch While You Eat' section would reduce anxiety about finding it again.
themes.implication: Supports a persistent placement/entry point rather than a one-off row, as a low-cost iteration.

themes.paraphrase: One respondent noted that some interactive elements (play buttons) weren't functional in the prototype.
themes.implication: Expected fake-door/prototype limitation, not a product signal.

core_kpis.name: Weekly Meal-Occasion Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of eligible respondents who watch something at a meal 3+ times a week.
core_kpis.source_question: pre_q1 — 'In a typical week, how many times do you watch on a streaming app while eating a meal?'
core_kpis.interpretation: Mealtime streaming is a frequent, recurring occasion for the large majority of eligible respondents, not an edge case.
core_kpis.limitation: Self-reported frequency band, not logged behaviour; bands are coarse (e.g. '3-5') so exact counts aren't recoverable.

core_kpis.name: High-Friction Decision Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of eligible respondents whose last mealtime decision took more than 3 minutes.
core_kpis.formula: n(decision_time in {3-5, 5-10, Over 10 minutes}) / n(eligible pre respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: pre — 'How long did you spend deciding before you actually started?'
core_kpis.interpretation: A majority spend more than 3 minutes deciding; the tail is meaningful too — 18.0% spend over 10 minutes.
core_kpis.limitation: Recall of a single past instance, not a timed measurement; 1 respondent who 'never started' is excluded from this rate.

core_kpis.name: Any-Abandonment Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of eligible respondents who gave up at least once in the last month after opening a streaming app at a meal.
core_kpis.formula: n(giveup_freq in {Once or twice, A few times, Often}) / n(eligible pre respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: pre — 'In the last month, how often did you open a streaming app at a meal but give up without watching anything?'
core_kpis.interpretation: Abandonment is broad at least-once, but the chronic form is narrow: only 13.1% report 'Often'. Report both — breadth is not the same as severity.
core_kpis.limitation: One-month recall window; no distinction between a 30-second reconsideration and a multi-minute abandoned search.

core_kpis.name: Off-Platform Leak Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of eligible respondents whose reported action, the last time deciding dragged, left Netflix (YouTube, social media, or another app) rather than staying on the platform.
core_kpis.formula: n(action_when_dragged in {YouTube, social media, another app}) / n(eligible pre respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: pre — 'The last time deciding dragged at a meal, what did you actually do?'
core_kpis.interpretation: YouTube alone accounts for 23 of 33 off-platform instances — the single largest destination and the clearest commercially relevant loss.
core_kpis.limitation: Question is framed around 'the last time deciding dragged', so it presupposes a drag event rather than being conditioned on the abandonment question (K3); not a strict funnel step.

core_kpis.name: Perceived Speed-Up Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents who rated finding something with the feature as faster or much faster than their normal routine.
core_kpis.formula: n(perceived_speed in {Faster, Much faster}) / n(post respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: post — "...finding something with the 'Watch While You Eat' row was..."
core_kpis.interpretation: A majority perceive a speed-up, but a large minority (about 4 in 10) felt no improvement or worse — this is a real, not unanimous, effect.
core_kpis.limitation: Stated perception in a single test session, not a timed A/B comparison against the normal routine.

core_kpis.name: Struggle Reduction Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents who said the feature reduced the 'what do I put on' struggle, clearly or somewhat.
core_kpis.formula: n(reduced_struggle in {Yes clearly, Somewhat}) / n(post respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: post — "Did it reduce the 'what do I put on' struggle for you specifically?"
core_kpis.interpretation: Very high on the surface, but only 21.6% chose the strong option ('Yes, clearly'); most of the 94.6% is the softer 'Somewhat'.
core_kpis.limitation: Self-report after a single short exposure; does not measure an actual repeated-use reduction in struggle.

core_kpis.name: Start-Intention Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents who said they would have started watching (easily or eventually) rather than probably given up, had this been a real meal.
core_kpis.formula: n(start_intention in {Started easily, Started eventually}) / n(post respondents)
core_kpis.source_question: post — 'If that had been a real meal just now, would you have started watching — or given up?'
core_kpis.interpretation: The strongest reaction measure in the study; directly answers the abandonment claim (C3) with a hypothetical intention, though only 45.9% chose the confident 'started easily' option.
core_kpis.limitation: Hypothetical/stated intention captured immediately after prototype exposure, not an observed behaviour at a real meal.

core_kpis.name: Retention Intention Rate
core_kpis.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents who said the feature would keep them on Netflix at a meal instead of switching, yes or maybe.
core_kpis.source_question: post — 'Would this keep you on Netflix at a meal instead of switching to something else?'
core_kpis.interpretation: Directly answers the C4 leak claim; among the matched respondents who had reported an off-platform leak pre-survey, 89.5% now say yes/maybe (n=19) — see matched analysis.
core_kpis.limitation: 'Maybe' (the largest single response) is counted toward retention; a stricter definition using only 'Yes' would give a materially lower rate — reported separately in the dashboard.

core_kpis.name: Top-Box Likelihood to Use
core_kpis.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents rating likelihood to use the feature at their next meal 8 or above out of 10.
core_kpis.source_question: post — 'How likely are you to use this at your next meal?' (0-10)
core_kpis.interpretation: The weakest of the reaction measures (mean 6.14, median 6.0) and the one requiring the most commitment from the respondent — this is the number the go/no-go decision should weight most heavily, not the softer reaction measures above.
core_kpis.limitation: Single-item stated intention; no observed repeat-use or actual adoption data exists to validate it against.

guardrail_kpi.name: Already-Seen / Would-Skip Rate
guardrail_kpi.definition: Share of post-prototype respondents who said the suggested episodes felt like content they'd already skip, rather than content they'd want.
guardrail_kpi.formula: n(guardrail_already_seen == "Mostly things I'd already skip") / n(post respondents who answered this item)
guardrail_kpi.source_question: post — "Of the episodes it suggested, did they feel like things you'd want, or things you'd already skip?"
guardrail_kpi.interpretation: No respondent chose the 'would already skip' pole; the split is 'Mostly things I'd want' (24/37) vs 'A mix' (13/37). No kill-switch signal in the current data — recommendation relevance is not failing outright.
guardrail_kpi.limitation: In the current Excel export this item has 0 missing values and real variance (unlike a prior report on this project, which flagged a related taste-match item as an unusable default value). Because a genuinely degenerate/default-only response pattern would invalidate this KPI, it should be re-checked against the live survey tool export (not just this snapshot) before being relied on for a go/no-go call.

notes: Spec S1/S2/S3 screener rules (age Under 18 or 31+; streaming freq Rarely; never watches while eating) match the screener independently recomputed in this analysis and reproduce the sheet's own screened_out flag exactly.

Spec's abandonment question (pre Q4) lists 5 options including 'Almost every time'; the export contains only 4 distinct values (Never / Once or twice / A few times / Often) — 'Almost every time' received zero responses in this dataset, it is not a missing category.
Spec's leak question (pre Q6) lists 6 options including 'Gave up and just ate'; the export contains only 5 distinct values — 'Gave up and just ate' received zero responses.
Spec's useful-components question (post Q6) lists a 'None' option; it does not appear in the export — every post respondent who answered selected at least one component as useful.

Spec's guardrail question (post Q5) options are 'Mostly want / A mix / Mostly already-seen or would-skip'; the export's two observed values ('Mostly things I'd want', 'A mix') match the spec's first two options, and zero respondents selected the failure option — consistent with the guardrail finding reported in Section 6 of the dashboard.

The post sheet contains one item — 'How well did the episodes it showed you match your taste?' (taste_match, scale 3-5) — that does NOT appear in the official post-survey question list (Q1-Q9) in the spec doc. It is treated here as a supplementary, non-spec item and reported separately (Section 4 / Section 6 of the dashboard), not folded into any spec-defined KPI.

The spec's own measurement-plan section refers to the likelihood-to-use top-box KPI as 'post_q9' while also defining Q9 as an open-text confusion question and Q7 (a 0-10 slider) as 'magnitude of relief' — an internal inconsistency in the spec document's question numbering. This analysis mapped columns by matching each column's actual header text to the closest spec question rather than by position/number, and used the column literally titled 'How likely are you to use this at your next meal?' as the likelihood-to-use KPI.

post 'stay_on_netflix' (leak-reversal) question: spec defines a single option 'No, I'd still switch'; the export splits this into two distinct values, 'No' (4 responses) and "I'd still switch" (1 response). Both are treated as non-retention for the Retention Intention KPI, consistent with either reading of the spec.

preregistered_behavioural_thresholds.source: Measurement Plan doc, section 2 (viability decision rule) — computed from an event log (row_impression, row_click, feature_dwell) this survey-only dataset does not contain; reported here for context on what 'validated' would require, not as a value computed here.
preregistered_behavioural_thresholds.feature_adoption_threshold: ≥30% of qualified sessions with ≥1 feature row click
preregistered_behavioural_thresholds.feature_dwell_threshold: ≥20 seconds median dwell among sessions that clicked the feature
preregistered_behavioural_thresholds.verdict_rule: validated only if all three hold; weak/inconclusive if uplift clears but dwell is low; not validated if uplift ≤1 or give-up dominates.

retention_and_clv_formulas_from_spec.retention_rate: (customers at end − new customers) ÷ customers at start × 100 — cannot be measured in a single-session fake-door test; use as the named business goal, with give-up rate and off-platform leak reported as its leading indicators.
retention_and_clv_formulas_from_spec.customer_lifetime_value: Margin × [ RR ÷ (1 + Discount − RR) ] — usable only as an illustrative, clearly-labelled sensitivity model, never as a measured value.
